body: Where I am going with this description of the paradigmatic position of the Slave, the World, and gratuitous violence is here:
the eviction
of Blackness/
Slaveness
from the Human fold
is constitutive of Black suffering
in a way
that cannot be reconciled with other paradigms of violence that subjugate other subaltern or degraded Humans,
and further, cannot have a sentence written about recourse or redress with the World.
And
any attempt to structurally adjust the condition of Black life
(a euphemism for captivity)
further obfuscates an honest perception of social death
, jettisoning a comprehensive understanding of enslavement’s totalizing violence.
The assumptive logics of Humanism, whereby all sentient beings suffer in the same ways plagues Western thought and has been rigorously critiqued and dispelled.
Through
critiquing the “universal” in the ways it imaginatively labors to reconcile or imagine the “unbridgeable crevice”
as commensurable, the works of Hortense Spillers, Saidiya Hartman, Zakiyyah Iman Jackson, Frank Wilderson, and Jared Sexton among others have
challenged
the notions of the universal not only in
its description, but also its prescription
, by pointing out where, how, and why these arguments falter
when encountering “the castigated particularity of the Slave
that shores up the universal.” Their critical interventions have
permitted the universalization of suffering
to be understood as symptomatic,
emblematic of what Wilderson
describes as the ruse of analogy

that “erroneously locates Blacks in the world—a place where they have not been since the dawning of Blackness” (p. 37). It is as though if Black suffering were to encapsulate the expanse of the universe, a particle moving at the speed of light would never reach its exteriority.

In this way, the ruse of analogy can be understood as an inadequately comparative analysis of the violence that situates the Slave (i.e., gratuitous violence) with the violence that situates those who are not slaves
(contingent violence). We might think of such an analogy as one that
mystifies the relation between the suffering that structures and saturates the
terrifyingly quotidian and ordinarily extreme
experiences of Black people with the suffering that structures other people’s lives
rather than clarifies the relation between social death and social life. This analogy
requires antiblackness to undergo a kind of adjustment
—structurally—
such that it looks like the suffering of subaltern violence

(e.g., heterosexist violence, gender violence, white supremacy), which is not to deny that it may share these attributes in important experiential ways, but to note that these apparent empirical similarities are analytically inessential.
However, what
a lens of analysis that attempts to
bear an explanatory power emphatic enough to
grasp the irreconcilability of
the structure of
power relations between the Black subject and everyone else
who is in fact a subject
might indicate
is
that while forms of degraded Humans
(e.g., nonblack women of color, nonblack queer people, nonblack undocumented immigrants, nonblack factory workers)
experience misery in
deeply insufferable
ways that take issues with aspects of the World
(e.g., patriarchy, capitalism, heterosexism), the Black subject—that is to
say the Slave—takes issue with the World and everyone else in it.
The nonblack subaltern is not attached to the ungendering, asignifying signifier of “cargo” in the collective unconscious.

This is verified anecdotally; it did not matter what a Black person identified as their gender; “men’s” and “women’s” bathrooms were not available to “Blacks,” who had to use dilapidated, non-facilities that were overridden with urine and feces to relieve themselves. The assumption was that
the category of gender can only be attached to Humans, the Slave experiencing the totality of abjection, is not recognized as a being of subjectivity to which categories of difference can cohere.
Hartman (1997) understands the way
Blackness as the frontier between property and person ruptures the normative understanding of gender and sexuality
in the context of the absence of consent, injury, and rape of the enslaved woman

as follows. The disregard of sexual injury does not divest slave women of gender but reveals the role of property relations—the possession of the enslaved, the making and exchange of human commodities, the harnessing of reproductive capacity, the inheritance and transmission of slave status through the maternal line, and the enjoyment of the thing—in the making of gender and sexuality

So, compared to subaltern conflicts wherein through struggle one can be “resuscitated” and that the performances of the of World can be improved and redeemable to the ethical dilemmas articulated by subaltern,
social death can neither be analogized with nor reduced to such paradigms of violence because
its mode of
redress
—a spatial or temporal concept that
makes the paradigm “sensibly coherent” such as “land” (the nonblack post-colonial subject) or
“owning one’s labor time” (the nonblack worker)—
cannot be articulated at all
. From the position adopted in this dissertation, we might consider the assumption that

the World holds the same redemptive promise for the Slave as anyone else analogizes the paradigm of violence of social death with other paradigms of violence that position the nonblack post-colonial subject, the nonblack gender oppressed subject, and the nonblack worker/subject. As I read it, this
ruse of analogy
clouds an understanding of the
paradigm of violence that banishes the Slave
from the World
and restricts
a comprehensive
understanding of Black suffering
in a way that conceals an understanding
that the capacity for subjectivity itself guarantees the Black subject
not among other contemporaries, but
an object among nonblack subjects
